title: Otitis Media in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Acute otitis media is a common bacterial infection of the middle ear in children, often following a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by otoscopy; treatment is usually antibiotics plus analgesia, with careful monitoring for complications.

sections.p: Acute otitis media (AOM) is inflammation of the middle ear with effusion and purulent discharge, usually bacterial, following a viral URI.
b: Classic triad: ear pain, fever, irritability in children

t.b: Shows bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane; a normal TM rules out AOM
Confirms bacterial etiology; guides antibiotic choice if resistant patterns are known

sections.p: Severity is graded by the presence of complications and systemic signs.
b: Moderate: persistent fever >39°C, vomiting, poor feeding
Severe: mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, or intracranial spread

sections.p: Bacterial pathogens dominate; viral causes are rare.

t.b: HIV‑positive children have higher rates of AOM and atypical pathogens

sections.p: Children present with ear pain, fever, irritability, and sometimes vomiting or refusal to eat.
b: Ear tugging or pulling in infants

sections.p: Most investigations are not required in low‑resource settings; focus on clinical exam.

t.b: A bulging, red TM with loss of landmarks indicates AOM
Normal temperature does not exclude AOM in young children
Detects hypoxaemia if complications like pneumonia develop

sections.p: Watch for signs of mastoiditis, facial nerve palsy, or intracranial spread.
Treat the infection, relieve pain, and monitor for complications.
b: If no improvement in 48–72h or worsening, re‑evaluate for complications

sections.p: Re‑assessment in 48–72h; prevention focuses on vaccination and hygiene.
b: Treating chronic adenoid hypertrophy if recurrent AOM

sections.p: Differential includes otitis externa, chronic otitis media, and ear trauma.
b: Ear trauma: history of injury, tympanic membrane perforation

sections.p: Normal tympanic membrane can mask AOM in infants; low-grade fever may be absent.
b: Fever may be absent in malnourished or immunocompromised children

whenToSeekHelp: Severe ear pain with fever >39°C and vomiting

faq.a: No, untreated AOM can lead to mastoiditis, hearing loss, and intracranial complications.

faq.q: When is a tympanostomy tube indicated?
faq.a: For recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months or ≥4 in 12 months) or persistent effusion causing hearing loss.

faq.q: Is a chest X‑ray needed for AOM?
faq.a: Only if there is suspicion of mastoiditis or intracranial spread; otherwise not required.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with ear pain and fever; otoscopy shows a bulging, erythematous TM. What is the first step in management? — Start amoxicillin; give analgesia; advise parents on ear protection.
A child with AOM has a fever that persists after 48h of antibiotics. What should you do? — Re‑evaluate for complications; consider changing antibiotic or adding a second agent.
A 4‑year‑old with AOM has a history of penicillin allergy. Which antibiotic is appropriate? — Amoxicillin‑clavulanate or cefuroxime.
A child with AOM develops a painless swelling behind the ear. What is the likely complication? — Mastoiditis; urgent ENT referral.
A 3‑month‑old infant has no fever but has ear tugging and irritability. Otoscopy shows a bulging TM. What is the diagnosis? — AOM; fever may be absent in infants.
A child with AOM has a normal tympanic membrane on otoscopy. What is the next step? — Consider otitis externa or chronic otitis media; repeat exam or refer.
A 5‑year‑old with recurrent AOM has hearing loss. What preventive measure is indicated? — Tympanostomy tubes and evaluation for adenoid hypertrophy.
A child with AOM is on amoxicillin but develops a rash. What is the likely cause? — Possible allergic reaction; stop antibiotic and consider alternative.
